RELIEF FROM A FAMILY LAW JUDGMENT AFTER SIX MONTHS (FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 2120-2129; VARNER; RUBENSTEIN; BREWER & FEDERICI; KIETURAKIS; GEORGIOU & LESLIE; BINETTE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PURPOSE AND IDENTIFICATION OF THE JUDGMENT
This document concerns the judgment entered on March 3, 2025 in the dissolution of marriage proceeding between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee (the "judgment"), and in particular the provisions of that judgment adjudicating the award of the employer pension plan and the equalizing payment. The circumstance said to bear on the judgment is described as: A retirement account not listed on either party's declaration of disclosure, first learned of on June 1, 2026. This document states legal background on the California statutes that govern when a court may relieve a spouse from a family law judgment adjudicating support or the division of property after the six-month period of Code of Civil Procedure section 473 has run -- Family Code sections 2120 through 2129 -- and on how the Courts of Appeal have applied those statutes in In re Marriage of Varner (1997), Rubenstein v. Rubenstein (2000), In re Marriage of Brewer & Federici (2001), In re Marriage of Kieturakis (2006), In re Marriage of Georgiou & Leslie (2013), and In re Marriage of Binette (2018). It is a companion to this project's Preliminary and Final Declarations of Disclosure, Section 2556 Omitted Community Property, and Section 1101 Fiduciary-Breach documents. This document is not a court order, is not a motion or pleading, and does not state whether any ground for relief exists or whether any request would be timely as to the judgment described above.

STATUTE: THE LEGISLATURE'S FINDINGS -- FULL DISCLOSURE, FINALITY, AND THE PRIOR "CONSIDERABLE CONFUSION"
Chapter 10 of Part 1 of Division 6 of the Family Code, titled "Relief From Judgment" (sections 2120 through 2129), opens with legislative findings. Section 2120 declares that California has a strong policy of ensuring the division of community and quasi-community property in a dissolution and of providing fair and sufficient child and spousal support awards, and that these goals can only be implemented with full disclosure of community, quasi-community, and separate assets, liabilities, income, and expenses, and with decisions freely and knowingly made. It acknowledges that it occasionally happens that a division of property or an award of support, whether made by agreement or after trial, is inequitable when made due to the nondisclosure or other misconduct of one of the parties; that the public policy of assuring finality of judgments must be balanced against the public interest in ensuring proper division of marital property, sufficient support awards, and deterrence of misconduct; and that the law governing when a judgment can be set aside after the time for relief under Code of Civil Procedure section 473 has passed had been the subject of considerable confusion leading to increased litigation and unpredictable and inconsistent decisions. In Rubenstein v. Rubenstein (2000), the Court of Appeal described the chapter as creating an exception to res judicata, grounded in the balance stated in subdivision (c).

STATUTE: RELIEF AFTER THE SIX-MONTH PERIOD OF CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE SECTION 473; THE TWO MATERIALITY FINDINGS; JUDGMENTS COVERED
Section 2121, subdivision (a), authorizes the court, in proceedings for dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, or legal separation, on any terms that may be just, to relieve a spouse from a judgment, or any part or parts of it, adjudicating support or division of property, after the six-month time limit of Code of Civil Procedure section 473 has run, based on the grounds and within the time limits provided in the chapter. Subdivision (b) adds a threshold for every such proceeding: before granting relief, the court must find that the facts alleged as the grounds for relief materially affected the original outcome and that the moving party would materially benefit from the granting of the relief. Section 2129 provides that the chapter applies to judgments entered on or after January 1, 1993. As the Court of Appeal summarized in In re Marriage of Kieturakis (2006), within six months after a marital dissolution judgment is taken, relief can be sought under Family Code section 2122 or Code of Civil Procedure section 473; after the six-month deadline of section 473 has passed, section 2122 specifies the exclusive grounds and time limits.

STATUTE AND CASE LAW: SIX EXCLUSIVE GROUNDS; ACTUAL FRAUD AND PERJURY WITHIN ONE YEAR OF DISCOVERY OF THE FACTS (RUBENSTEIN)
Section 2122 states that the grounds and time limits for a motion to set aside a judgment, or any part or parts of it, are governed by that section and "shall be one of" the grounds it lists. As the Court of Appeal summarized in In re Marriage of Binette (2018), there are six: actual fraud, perjury, duress, mental incapacity, mistake, or failure to comply with the disclosure requirements. The first two carry a discovery-based one-year limit. Under subdivision (a), the ground is actual fraud where the defrauded party was kept in ignorance or in some other manner was fraudulently prevented from fully participating in the proceeding, and an action or motion based on fraud must be brought within one year after the date on which the complaining party either did discover, or should have discovered, the fraud. Under subdivision (b), the ground is perjury in the preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, the waiver of the final declaration of disclosure, or the current income and expense statement, with the same one-year-from-discovery limit. In Rubenstein v. Rubenstein (2000), the Court of Appeal reasoned by analogy to Code of Civil Procedure section 338, subdivision (d), and held that the one-year period accrues when the complaining party discovered or should have discovered the facts constituting the fraud or perjury, not the date the party began to suspect it; the court added that a spouse who conceals the existence of community assets, thereby depriving the other spouse of the opportunity fully to present his or her case, cannot claim the judgment is conclusive and immune from subsequent attack. Rubenstein and Brewer & Federici also record that, before the chapter was enacted, only "extrinsic" fraud -- not "intrinsic" fraud such as perjury -- could support relief after the section 473 period, and that the statutory scheme abolished that distinction.

STATUTE: DURESS AND MENTAL INCAPACITY -- TWO YEARS FROM ENTRY OF JUDGMENT
Two of the six grounds run from the date the judgment was entered rather than from discovery. Under section 2122, subdivision (c), an action or motion based upon duress must be brought within two years after the date of entry of judgment. Under subdivision (d), an action or motion based on mental incapacity must likewise be brought within two years after the date of entry of judgment. The statute does not define either term. In In re Marriage of Binette (2018), the former wife's request to set aside a default judgment incorporating a marital settlement agreement invoked subdivisions (d) and (e), supported by her own declaration and a physician's declaration that she suffered from depression associated with significant cognitive impairment; the trial court granted the request on the ground of mistake of fact rather than mental incapacity, and the Court of Appeal affirmed on that ground.

STATUTE AND CASE LAW: MISTAKE IN A STIPULATED OR UNCONTESTED JUDGMENT -- ONE YEAR FROM ENTRY; VARNER (NONDISCLOSURE OF AN ASSET'S EXISTENCE OR VALUE IS A "MISTAKE")
Section 2122, subdivision (e), applies only to stipulated or uncontested judgments, or to that part of a judgment stipulated to by the parties. As to those, the ground is mistake, either mutual or unilateral, whether mistake of law or mistake of fact, and an action or motion based on mistake must be brought within one year after the date of entry of judgment. In In re Marriage of Varner (1997), the first published decision construing the chapter, a former wife who had been unrepresented at the hearing moved within a year to set aside a stipulated judgment after obtaining appraisals indicating that the businesses and real property awarded to her former husband, which he had testified were worth about zero or far less, were worth millions. The Court of Appeal reversed the denial of her motion. It reasoned that under the stringent "extrinsic mistake" standard that would have applied before the statutory changes, the facts might not have warranted reversal, but that the newly enacted requirements of full disclosure changed the analysis: like perjury, a failure to disclose would induce the other spouse to stipulate to a judgment on the basis of incomplete or inaccurate information. The court concluded that the failure of a spouse to disclose the existence or the value of a community asset constitutes a basis for setting aside a judgment on the ground of mistake under section 2122.

CASE LAW: BREWER & FEDERICI -- UNILATERAL MISTAKE WITHOUT WRONGDOING; LISTING A MAJOR ASSET'S VALUE AS "UNKNOWN"; THE BETTER-POSITIONED SPOUSE'S DUTY TO OBTAIN VALUATION INFORMATION
In In re Marriage of Brewer & Federici (2001), the parties' final declarations of disclosure listed the wife's employer pension as "unknown" in value and her savings program at an outdated figure of $168,561 taken from a statement more than a year old; the husband understood there to be one plan worth about $170,000 and agreed to a global settlement, including an equalizing payment to the wife, on that basis. The two plans were in fact worth more than $500,000, almost all community property. The trial court set aside the judgment and the marital settlement agreement (except as to marital status) for mistake under section 2122, subdivision (e), and the Court of Appeal affirmed. The court held that the lack of full and accurate disclosure may be grounds for relief based upon mistake; that a marital settlement agreement is not an arm's-length transaction between adversaries but the result of negotiations between fiduciaries required to openly share information; that the wife's arguments failed to address the court's ability to grant relief based upon mistake regardless of a finding of wrongdoing; and that, where the asset was one of the largest community assets, financial in nature, and easily valued, stating its value as "unknown" was not sufficient disclosure. Rejecting the argument that the husband had neglected his own duty to value the plans, the court reasoned that a spouse in a superior position to obtain records or information from which an asset can be valued, who can reasonably do so, must acquire and disclose that information to the other spouse, and that the other spouse is entitled to rely on the information provided. The court added that spouses remain free to agree to an unequal division, so long as the agreement rests on a complete and accurate understanding of the existence and value of the assets material to it.

STATUTE AND CASE LAW: FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH THE DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS -- ONE YEAR FROM DISCOVERY (ADDED 2001); BINETTE (A DEFECTIVE WAIVER OF FINAL DISCLOSURE)
The sixth ground, subdivision (f) of section 2122, is failure to comply with the disclosure requirements of Chapter 9 of the same Part (sections 2100 through 2113, the preliminary and final declarations of disclosure). An action or motion on this ground must be brought within one year after the date on which the complaining party either discovered, or should have discovered, the failure to comply. As In re Marriage of Georgiou & Leslie (2013) explains, the Legislature added this ground in 2001, after Varner and Brewer & Federici had reached nondisclosure through the "mistake" ground. In In re Marriage of Binette (2018), the parties had filed a stipulation waiving final declarations of disclosure that recited that preliminary declarations had been completed and exchanged; in fact the husband's preliminary declaration lacked supporting documents and the wife had never completed or exchanged any declaration at all. Quoting In re Marriage of Burkle (2006), the Court of Appeal stated that the mandatory disclosure requirements cannot be waived except in strict compliance with the statute, held that the stipulation was insufficient to act as a waiver of final disclosure given the lack of compliance, and affirmed the order vacating the default judgment on the ground that the parties had been mistaken about whether the statutory requirements had been satisfied.

CASE LAW: KIETURAKIS -- THE MOVING PARTY BEARS THE BURDEN OF PROOF; THE PRESUMPTION OF UNDUE INFLUENCE DOES NOT SHIFT IT FOR A MEDIATED SETTLEMENT OR A JUDGMENT AT LEAST SIX MONTHS OLD
In In re Marriage of Kieturakis (2006), a former wife moved under section 2122 to set aside a judgment incorporating a marital settlement agreement reached in mediation, alleging fraud, duress, and lack of disclosure, while refusing to waive the mediation privilege. The trial court, finding that the agreement favored the former husband, applied the presumption of undue influence that attaches to interspousal transactions advantaging one spouse and placed on him the burden of proving the absence of duress, fraud, or perjury. The Court of Appeal held that he should not have been made to bear that burden, for three independently sufficient reasons. First, the presumption of undue influence cannot be applied to marital settlement agreements reached through mediation, because doing so would turn the shield of mediation confidentiality into a sword by which any unequal agreement could be invalidated. Second, there is no precedent for applying the presumption in a section 2122 motion, and those seeking to set aside judgments have always borne the burden of proof; the policy favoring finality of judgments militates strongly in favor of keeping that burden with the moving party, at least where relief is sought after the time to act under Code of Civil Procedure section 473 has expired. The court accordingly concluded that a party seeking relief from a judgment that incorporates an unequal marital settlement agreement must bear the burden of proof under section 2122, at least where the judgment is at least six months old. Third, the parties' own recitals in the agreement that it was entered voluntarily, free from duress, fraud, undue influence, coercion, or misrepresentation, with the requisite disclosures exchanged, negated the presumption, at least where capacity was not in question.

STATUTE: ATTORNEY NEGLIGENCE NOT IMPUTED; PARTIAL SET-ASIDE; VALUATION AND DIVISION OF AFFECTED ASSETS; STATEMENT OF DECISION (SECTIONS 2124-2127)
Four further sections govern the mechanics of relief. Section 2124 provides that the negligence of an attorney is not imputed to a client to bar an order setting aside a judgment, unless the court finds that the client knew, or should have known, of the attorney's negligence and unreasonably failed to self-protect. Section 2125 directs that, when ruling on an action or motion to set aside a judgment, the court set aside only those provisions materially affected by the circumstances leading to its decision to grant relief, while preserving the court's discretion to set aside the entire judgment if necessary for equitable considerations. Section 2126 provides that, as to assets or liabilities for which a judgment or part of a judgment is set aside, the date of valuation is subject to equitable considerations, and that the court shall equally divide the asset or liability unless it finds upon good cause shown that the interests of justice require an unequal division; Rubenstein described this as empowering the court, upon vacating the judgment in whole or in part, to make an unequal distribution of the concealed assets in the interests of justice. Section 2127 requires the court, on a timely request, to render a statement of decision where it has resolved controverted factual evidence. In Brewer & Federici, the trial court set aside the judgment and settlement agreement in their entirety except as to marital status, reasoning that it would be illogical and unlawful to hold either party to an agreement made without full disclosure or to allow either party to choose which portions to set aside.

Chapter 10 of Part 1 of Division 6 of the Family Code, titled "Relief From Judgment" (sections 2120 through 2129), opens with legislative findings. Section 2120 declares that California has a strong policy of ensuring the division of community and quasi-community property in a dissolution and of providing fair and sufficient child and spousal support awards, and that these goals can only be implemented with full disclosure of community, quasi-community, and separate assets, liabilities, income, and expenses, and with decisions freely and knowingly made. It acknowledges that it occasionally happens that a division of property or an award of support, whether made by agreement or after trial, is inequitable when made due to the nondisclosure or other misconduct of one of the parties; that the public policy of assuring finality of judgments must be balanced against the public interest in ensuring proper division of marital property, sufficient support awards, and deterrence of misconduct; and that the law governing when a judgment can be set aside after the time for relief under Code of Civil Procedure section 473 has passed had been the subject of considerable confusion leading to increased litigation and unpredictable and inconsistent decisions. In Rubenstein v. Rubenstein (2000), the Court of Appeal described the chapter as creating an exception to res judicata, grounded in the balance stated in subdivision (c).

expectedJSON.body: Section 2122 states that the grounds and time limits for a motion to set aside a judgment, or any part or parts of it, are governed by that section and "shall be one of" the grounds it lists. As the Court of Appeal summarized in In re Marriage of Binette (2018), there are six: actual fraud, perjury, duress, mental incapacity, mistake, or failure to comply with the disclosure requirements. The first two carry a discovery-based one-year limit. Under subdivision (a), the ground is actual fraud where the defrauded party was kept in ignorance or in some other manner was fraudulently prevented from fully participating in the proceeding, and an action or motion based on fraud must be brought within one year after the date on which the complaining party either did discover, or should have discovered, the fraud. Under subdivision (b), the ground is perjury in the preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, the waiver of the final declaration of disclosure, or the current income and expense statement, with the same one-year-from-discovery limit. In Rubenstein v. Rubenstein (2000), the Court of Appeal reasoned by analogy to Code of Civil Procedure section 338, subdivision (d), and held that the one-year period accrues when the complaining party discovered or should have discovered the facts constituting the fraud or perjury, not the date the party began to suspect it; the court added that a spouse who conceals the existence of community assets, thereby depriving the other spouse of the opportunity fully to present his or her case, cannot claim the judgment is conclusive and immune from subsequent attack. Rubenstein and Brewer & Federici also record that, before the chapter was enacted, only "extrinsic" fraud -- not "intrinsic" fraud such as perjury -- could support relief after the section 473 period, and that the statutory scheme abolished that distinction.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2122, subdivision (e), applies only to stipulated or uncontested judgments, or to that part of a judgment stipulated to by the parties. As to those, the ground is mistake, either mutual or unilateral, whether mistake of law or mistake of fact, and an action or motion based on mistake must be brought within one year after the date of entry of judgment. In In re Marriage of Varner (1997), the first published decision construing the chapter, a former wife who had been unrepresented at the hearing moved within a year to set aside a stipulated judgment after obtaining appraisals indicating that the businesses and real property awarded to her former husband, which he had testified were worth about zero or far less, were worth millions. The Court of Appeal reversed the denial of her motion. It reasoned that under the stringent "extrinsic mistake" standard that would have applied before the statutory changes, the facts might not have warranted reversal, but that the newly enacted requirements of full disclosure changed the analysis: like perjury, a failure to disclose would induce the other spouse to stipulate to a judgment on the basis of incomplete or inaccurate information. The court concluded that the failure of a spouse to disclose the existence or the value of a community asset constitutes a basis for setting aside a judgment on the ground of mistake under section 2122.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Brewer & Federici (2001), the parties' final declarations of disclosure listed the wife's employer pension as "unknown" in value and her savings program at an outdated figure of $168,561 taken from a statement more than a year old; the husband understood there to be one plan worth about $170,000 and agreed to a global settlement, including an equalizing payment to the wife, on that basis. The two plans were in fact worth more than $500,000, almost all community property. The trial court set aside the judgment and the marital settlement agreement (except as to marital status) for mistake under section 2122, subdivision (e), and the Court of Appeal affirmed. The court held that the lack of full and accurate disclosure may be grounds for relief based upon mistake; that a marital settlement agreement is not an arm's-length transaction between adversaries but the result of negotiations between fiduciaries required to openly share information; that the wife's arguments failed to address the court's ability to grant relief based upon mistake regardless of a finding of wrongdoing; and that, where the asset was one of the largest community assets, financial in nature, and easily valued, stating its value as "unknown" was not sufficient disclosure. Rejecting the argument that the husband had neglected his own duty to value the plans, the court reasoned that a spouse in a superior position to obtain records or information from which an asset can be valued, who can reasonably do so, must acquire and disclose that information to the other spouse, and that the other spouse is entitled to rely on the information provided. The court added that spouses remain free to agree to an unequal division, so long as the agreement rests on a complete and accurate understanding of the existence and value of the assets material to it.

expectedJSON.body: The sixth ground, subdivision (f) of section 2122, is failure to comply with the disclosure requirements of Chapter 9 of the same Part (sections 2100 through 2113, the preliminary and final declarations of disclosure). An action or motion on this ground must be brought within one year after the date on which the complaining party either discovered, or should have discovered, the failure to comply. As In re Marriage of Georgiou & Leslie (2013) explains, the Legislature added this ground in 2001, after Varner and Brewer & Federici had reached nondisclosure through the "mistake" ground. In In re Marriage of Binette (2018), the parties had filed a stipulation waiving final declarations of disclosure that recited that preliminary declarations had been completed and exchanged; in fact the husband's preliminary declaration lacked supporting documents and the wife had never completed or exchanged any declaration at all. Quoting In re Marriage of Burkle (2006), the Court of Appeal stated that the mandatory disclosure requirements cannot be waived except in strict compliance with the statute, held that the stipulation was insufficient to act as a waiver of final disclosure given the lack of compliance, and affirmed the order vacating the default judgment on the ground that the parties had been mistaken about whether the statutory requirements had been satisfied.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Kieturakis (2006), a former wife moved under section 2122 to set aside a judgment incorporating a marital settlement agreement reached in mediation, alleging fraud, duress, and lack of disclosure, while refusing to waive the mediation privilege. The trial court, finding that the agreement favored the former husband, applied the presumption of undue influence that attaches to interspousal transactions advantaging one spouse and placed on him the burden of proving the absence of duress, fraud, or perjury. The Court of Appeal held that he should not have been made to bear that burden, for three independently sufficient reasons. First, the presumption of undue influence cannot be applied to marital settlement agreements reached through mediation, because doing so would turn the shield of mediation confidentiality into a sword by which any unequal agreement could be invalidated. Second, there is no precedent for applying the presumption in a section 2122 motion, and those seeking to set aside judgments have always borne the burden of proof; the policy favoring finality of judgments militates strongly in favor of keeping that burden with the moving party, at least where relief is sought after the time to act under Code of Civil Procedure section 473 has expired. The court accordingly concluded that a party seeking relief from a judgment that incorporates an unequal marital settlement agreement must bear the burden of proof under section 2122, at least where the judgment is at least six months old. Third, the parties' own recitals in the agreement that it was entered voluntarily, free from duress, fraud, undue influence, coercion, or misrepresentation, with the requisite disclosures exchanged, negated the presumption, at least where capacity was not in question.

expectedJSON.body: Four further sections govern the mechanics of relief. Section 2124 provides that the negligence of an attorney is not imputed to a client to bar an order setting aside a judgment, unless the court finds that the client knew, or should have known, of the attorney's negligence and unreasonably failed to self-protect. Section 2125 directs that, when ruling on an action or motion to set aside a judgment, the court set aside only those provisions materially affected by the circumstances leading to its decision to grant relief, while preserving the court's discretion to set aside the entire judgment if necessary for equitable considerations. Section 2126 provides that, as to assets or liabilities for which a judgment or part of a judgment is set aside, the date of valuation is subject to equitable considerations, and that the court shall equally divide the asset or liability unless it finds upon good cause shown that the interests of justice require an unequal division; Rubenstein described this as empowering the court, upon vacating the judgment in whole or in part, to make an unequal distribution of the concealed assets in the interests of justice. Section 2127 requires the court, on a timely request, to render a statement of decision where it has resolved controverted factual evidence. In Brewer & Federici, the trial court set aside the judgment and settlement agreement in their entirety except as to marital status, reasoning that it would be illogical and unlawful to hold either party to an agreement made without full disclosure or to allow either party to choose which portions to set aside.

expectedJSON.body: Rubenstein v. Rubenstein (2000) held that the remedy under the chapter is a traditional setting aside of the judgment, and that no tort action lies for concealment of community assets in a dissolution proceeding; the court declared the contrary holding of Dale v. Dale (1998) no longer operative for judgments the chapter governs, and concluded that section 2122 governed the former wife's action in its entirety irrespective of the various legal theories pleaded. The court found support in section 2128, which lists what the chapter does not disturb: relief under section 2556 for omitted or unadjudicated community assets; existing contract remedies where the contract has not been merged or incorporated into a judgment; the family law court's power to act as a court of equity; existing law on modification or enforcement of support orders; and the rights of a bona fide lessee, purchaser, or encumbrancer for value of real property. Applying the maxim that the expression of certain things excludes others, the court read that enumeration as excluding remedies not specified. In In re Marriage of Georgiou & Leslie (2013), a former wife who learned of an undervalued referral fee more than a year before suing brought a post-judgment action for breach of fiduciary duty under section 1101 instead of a section 2122 motion. The Court of Appeal held that section 1101 did not authorize a post-judgment action in those circumstances, because the fee could not be disposed of without upsetting the judgment or at least a portion of it; that her exclusive remedy was a set-aside action under section 2122; and that, because she did not file within the one-year period of subdivision (f), the family court lacked jurisdiction over the matter.
